content: Lung edema can complicate respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in preterm infants, potentially worsening their condition. This review aimed to evaluate the risks and benefits of administering diuretics to preterm infants with RDS. To gather relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE databases. These searches were updated periodically in April 2003, March 2007, January 2011, and August 2011. Additional searches included abstract books from the American Thoracic Society and the Society for Pediatric Research, as well as databases like controlled-trials.com and clinicaltrials.gov. The keyword Respiratory Distress Syndrome was used to identify studies involving medications recently classified as diuretics, such as theophylline. The review included randomized controlled trials involving preterm infants with RDS who were less than five days old. To be eligible, studies had to evaluate at least one of the following outcomes: mortality, patent ductus arteriosus, hypovolemic shock, intraventricular hemorrhage, renal failure, duration of oxygen supplementation, duration of mechanical ventilation, need for oxygen supplementation at 28 days of life, oxygen supplementation at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age, length of hospital stay, number of rehospitalizations during the first year of life, or neurodevelopmental outcomes. Data collection and analysis followed the standard methods outlined in the Cochrane Collaboration Handbook. Two investigators independently extracted, assessed, and coded data from each study, resolving any disagreements through discussion. Seven studies met the inclusion criteria. Six of these studies, which investigated the use of furosemide, were conducted before the widespread use of prenatal steroids, surfactant therapy, and fluid restriction. Furosemide administration showed no long-term benefits. While it transiently improved pulmonary function, this benefit was outweighed by an increased risk of patent ductus arteriosus and hemodynamic instability. A more recent study on theophylline also demonstrated no long-term benefits. Although theophylline significantly reduced the risk of oligoanuria and temporarily improved renal function, it did not have a significant impact on renal function at discharge or other clinical outcomes. The authors concluded that there is no evidence to support the routine use of furosemide in preterm infants with RDS. The elective use of furosemide should be carefully considered, as it carries risks such as hypovolemia and symptomatic patent ductus arteriosus. Similarly, there is insufficient evidence to recommend the routine administration of low-dose theophylline in this population.
